notes.name: Two-Level SOP Network
notes.description: AND-plane feeding one OR gate: minimum logic depth 2 for any function, paid for in unbounded fan-in and literal count.

notes.name: Two-Level POS Network
notes.description: OR-plane feeding one AND gate: the dual realization, natural when the function has few zeros.

notes.name: NAND-NAND Network
notes.description: Every AND and the OR of a two-level SOP replaced by NAND at identical gate count and depth, deleting one inverter per gate on a static CMOS target.

notes.name: NOR-NOR Network
notes.description: The POS dual of NAND-NAND; correct and free in algebra, but slower in CMOS because NOR series-stacks the PMOS devices.

notes.name: Multi-Level Factored Network
notes.description: Factoring and shared subexpressions trade one or more levels of depth for large literal-count reductions that two-level minimization cannot find.

notes.name: Shannon Expansion Multiplexer
notes.description: Any function is a 2:1 mux on one variable selecting its two cofactors; recursing gives the mux tree and the LUT decomposition.

notes.name: Karnaugh Map
notes.description: Gray-coded truth table where adjacency is absorption; circling prime implicants yields a minimal two-level cover by eye up to four variables.

notes.name: Binary Decoder
notes.description: Turns an n-bit code into one-hot 2^n select lines in a single AND level; costs n*2^n gate inputs and n-input ANDs that stop being buildable past n=4.

notes.name: Predecoder
notes.description: Two half-width decoders ANDed pairwise: every gate becomes an AND2 and gate-input count drops from n*2^n to O(2^n), the factoring an SRAM row decoder actually uses.

notes.name: Demultiplexer
notes.description: Routes one data bit to one of 2^n outputs: a decoder plus 2^n AND2s, one level deeper than the decoder it wraps.

notes.name: Binary Encoder
notes.description: Inverse of a decoder as a wire-OR, log-depth and nearly free — but correct only on genuinely one-hot input, where two hot bits silently emit a third valid address.

notes.name: Priority Encoder
notes.description: Removes the one-hot precondition by returning the index of the highest set bit; the naive ripple of length 2^n reassociates into a log-depth prefix-OR plus mask plus plain encoder.

notes.name: Multiplexer Tree
notes.description: 2^n-1 MUX2s in n levels: no gate ever exceeds two inputs, depth grows as log, and it is the only mux form that scales past n=3 without an unbuildable gate.
source_headings: ## Shannon expansion: every function is a mux tree
## Worked example: a 4:1 multiplexer, two ways

notes.name: One-Hot Multiplexer
notes.description: Decode the select and drive a flat AND-OR: two levels on paper, but a 2^n-wide OR and a branched select path make it slower than the deeper tree above 4:1.
source_headings: ## Worked example: a 4:1 multiplexer, two ways

notes.name: Transmission-Gate Multiplexer
notes.description: Two transmission gates and an inverter, 6 transistors instead of ~12 static CMOS — but series stages form an RC ladder whose delay grows quadratically, so buffer every two or three levels.

notes.name: XOR Parity Tree
notes.description: n-1 XOR2s reassociated from a chain into a balanced tree: log depth for free, but XOR is the worst static gate there is (g=4, p=4) so the cost is gates, not levels.

notes.name: Logic Hazards
notes.description: Static-1, static-0 and dynamic glitches on a single input change: artefacts of the netlist, not the function, and the reason a correct truth table can still burn 20-40% of its energy on transients.

notes.name: Hazard-Free Two-Level Cover
notes.description: Add the consensus term for every adjacent pair of ON-set cells: logically redundant area bought purely for a timing property, and the only hazard repair with a clean K-map criterion.
source_headings: ## Worked example: a 4:1 multiplexer, two ways

notes.name: Logical Effort
notes.description: d = g·h + p prices fan-in properly, gives D_min = N·F^(1/N) + P and the FO4 yardstick, and explains why a shallower flat netlist can be the slower one.
notes.spade_note: A transistor-level delay model — it prices netlists, it does not synthesise to one.
source_headings: ## Worked example: a 4:1 multiplexer, two ways

notes.name: Cross-Coupled Inverter Bistable
notes.description: Two inverters in a loop store a bit forever for free; the loop-gain criterion gives two stable states and the unstable point where metastability lives.
notes.spade_note: Combinational feedback. `let v1 = inv(v2); let v2 = inv(v1);` fails with "Use of undeclared name" — Spade `let` cannot self-reference and there is no latch primitive.

notes.name: SR Latch
notes.description: Cheapest writeable bistable: two cross-coupled NORs, one set input, one reset — and one forbidden input code whose release is an unarbitrated race.
notes.spade_note: Combinational feedback: Q depends on ~Q depends on Q. `let q = nor(r, qb);` cannot be closed in Spade — no latch primitive, `let` cannot self-reference.

notes.name: Transparent D Latch
notes.description: Tie R to the complement of S and the forbidden state vanishes: a 2:1 mux whose select is the clock and whose feedback leg is the hold path, 8-12 transistors, transparent for a whole phase.
notes.spade_note: The hold leg is combinational feedback: `let q = if clk { d } else { q };` errors with "Use of undeclared name q". Passing q in as a port compiles but yields a mux, not a latch.

notes.name: Switch Debouncer
notes.description: The one place the SR latch's forbidden state is unreachable by construction: an SPDT contact physically cannot assert both inputs, so bounce becomes a clean single transition with no clock and no filter.
notes.spade_note: Built on the SR latch, so the same combinational-feedback limit applies. The synchronous alternative — a counter-based debouncer on a slow clock — is expressible and is the version the note should show as the nearest Spade structure.

notes.name: Master-Slave D Flip-Flop
notes.description: Two opposite-phase latches that are never transparent at the same instant, buying the hard clock edge that collapses timing to two checkable inequalities — for 20-26 transistors and four clocked loads per bit.

notes.name: JK Flip-Flop
notes.description: Hold/set/reset/toggle in one cell, whose excitation table is half don't-cares — free literals under K-map minimization when gates were DIP pins, and dead weight in a standard-cell library.
source_headings: ## JK and T flip-flops, and why they are historical

notes.name: T Flip-Flop
notes.description: An XOR in front of a D flop: toggles on command, still the right structure for a counter bit even though no library carries it as a cell.
source_headings: ## JK and T flip-flops, and why they are historical

notes.name: Setup and Hold Constraints
notes.description: The aperture window around the edge, and the two inequalities it produces — one you can buy with frequency and one you cannot, which is why hold failures are dead silicon and setup failures are just a slower part.
notes.spade_note: A timing-analysis relation between characterized cell parameters, not a structure. The launch-logic-capture path it constrains is drawn, but the note's content is the inequality.
source_headings: ## Setup, hold, clock-to-Q, and the aperture window

notes.name: Clock Skew and Jitter
notes.description: Spatial-static versus temporal-random error on the same edge: skew is signed, budgetable and exploitable, jitter is not, and only one of them can eat your hold margin.
notes.spade_note: A property of the clock distribution network and its variation, not an RTL structure. The H-tree that bounds it is physical design.

notes.name: Synchronizer Chain
notes.description: N flops in series with nothing between them, buying a factor of exp(T_clk/tau) of MTBF per stage — a few square microns for five orders of magnitude, and the only lever with that leverage.

notes.name: Clock Enable Flip-Flop
notes.description: A 2:1 mux in the D path to hold a value: timing-safe and free on an FPGA's dedicated CE pin, but on an ASIC it taxes the critical path every cycle and saves no clock power.

notes.name: Integrated Clock-Gating Cell
notes.description: A low-phase latch feeding an AND — the latch is not optional, it is what stops a glitch on the enable from becoming a spurious clock edge; the largest dynamic-power lever in a synchronous design.
notes.spade_note: Two reasons: the glitch-suppressing element is a level-sensitive latch (combinational feedback), and Spade's `clock` type is not a value that can be ANDed with data. The note shows `if en { ... }` and states that synthesis, not RTL, chooses the gating cell.

notes.name: Two-Phase Latch Pipeline
notes.description: Alternating phi1/phi2 transparent-latch banks on a half-period grid with logic between them; removes the per-stage max from the cycle-time constraint at the cost of dual CTS, tool friction and a lost cycle boundary.
notes.spade_note: The pipeline is built from level-sensitive transparent D latches. Spade has no latch primitive and `let q = if en { d } else { q };` fails with "Use of undeclared name q", so the transparency window cannot be described at all.

notes.name: Non-Overlapping Two-Phase Clock Generator
notes.description: Cross-coupled NAND pair with delay chains producing phi1/phi2 with a tunable dead gap t_nov; the gap buys hold margin picosecond for picosecond out of the borrow budget B.
notes.spade_note: Cross-coupled NAND cell is combinational feedback (each gate's output feeds the other's input with no clock between), and the delay-chain legs have no Spade expression.

notes.name: Pulsed Latch
notes.description: One transparent latch on the full-cycle grid clocked by a narrow pulse; buys a t_p - t_su - t_sk borrow window with a flop-like interface for STA, scan and LEC — the settlement nearly every high-frequency team lands on.
notes.spade_note: Level-sensitive latch core; the pulse only narrows the transparency window, it does not make the cell clocked in the reg(clk) sense.

notes.name: Clock Pulse Generator
notes.description: Delay chain plus AND producing the narrow t_p pulse for a pulsed-latch cluster; area and clock energy are amortised over the latches it drives, and its width sets both the borrow window and the hold requirement.
notes.spade_note: Relies on gate delay: `clk & !delay(clk)` has no Spade expression — there is no delay primitive, and the un-delayed form constant-folds to 0. Different language limit from combinational feedback; see report.

notes.name: Clock-Gated Latch Bank
notes.description: Latch bank whose enable is implemented by gating one phase's clock; cheapest variant measured (-29.2 % power, -50 % latch count vs recirculation mux) but the gate sits in one tree only, producing 2.63 ns skew against 0.18 ns.
notes.spade_note: Level-sensitive latch storage element; Spade has no latch primitive, and gating a clock net is outside the language's clock model regardless.
source_headings: EDA tool support — the real answer

notes.name: Recirculating-Mux Latch Bank
notes.description: Latch bank holding state by muxing Q back to D instead of gating the clock; keeps both clock trees symmetric (0.18 ns skew) but costs +299 % sequential cells and +142.7 % power, and failed to route on JPEG at 17325 latches.
notes.spade_note: The recirculation mux closes a combinational loop through a transparent latch; both the latch and the loop are outside the language.

notes.name: LSSD Scan Latch Pair
notes.description: IBM's L1/L2 pair used as its own scan cell with separate system and non-overlapping scan clocks A and B; race- and hazard-free in both modes, and the reason two-phase DFT is the one genuinely solved part of the flow.
notes.spade_note: Two level-sensitive latches with multiple clock ports; neither the latch nor the multi-clock scan structure exists in Spade.
source_headings: EDA tool support — the real answer

notes.name: Programmable Local Clock Buffer
notes.description: POWER6's C1/C2 local clock buffer with delay-C1 cycle-stealing mode and three selectable pulse widths (2.9/4.2/5.2 FO4), so cycle boundaries can be moved in hardware to tune frequency after fabrication.
notes.spade_note: Pulse chopper and programmable delay legs on the clock path; no Spade construct describes a delay element or a locally derived clock phase.

notes.name: Canonical FSM Structure
notes.description: The three-block template every state machine reduces to — next-state logic, state register, output logic — with the critical path living only in the q-to-delta-to-q loop.

notes.name: Moore Machine
notes.description: Output is a function of state alone, so it is a registered signal in all but name — glitch-free and safe to use as an enable, at the cost of one cycle and one extra state.

notes.name: Mealy Machine
notes.description: Output is a function of state and current input, answering one cycle earlier with strictly fewer states, but adding a combinational x-to-z path that chains across cascaded machines and tracks every input glitch.

notes.name: State Transition Graph
notes.description: The machine as a labelled digraph and its state table; once encoded the table is literally a truth table, and the completeness and determinism checks are what stop synthesis inferring a latch.
source_headings: ## State transition graphs and state tables

notes.name: Binary State Encoding
notes.description: Minimum flop count at ceil(log2 N) bits, paying for it with next-state fan-in that grows as log2 N + k and a separate minimization per state bit.

notes.name: One-Hot State Encoding
notes.description: One flop per state, next-state equation transcribed straight from incoming edges, giving fan-in equal to in-degree and therefore flat in N — the reason FPGA tools default to it above ~16 states.

notes.name: Gray Code State Encoding
notes.description: Same width as binary with single-bit transitions, worth the effort only for chain-shaped machines or a state bus sampled from another clock domain where at most one bit may be metastable.

notes.name: Safe-State FSM Recovery
notes.description: Reset coverage, a default arm that synthesis will delete unless attributed, and a decoded one-hot legality check — the four escalating costs of guaranteeing the machine leaves an unused code.

notes.name: FSMD Controller-Datapath Split
notes.description: Wide data in registers and operators, narrow schedule in a control FSM, so an 8-bit accumulator is one register instead of 256 states — and the status-flag-to-control-word loop becomes the critical path.

notes.name: Pipeline Register Insertion
notes.description: Cutting a feed-forward path with p register stages trades p cycles of latency for a p-fold cycle-time reduction — and is exactly what you cannot do to next-state logic, because a register inside the loop builds a different machine.

notes.name: Retiming
notes.description: Moving existing registers across gates without changing I/O behaviour, bounded by register conservation around every directed cycle — which is why no retiming makes an FSM faster than its next-state logic.

notes.name: C-Slow Retiming
notes.description: Replace every register with C in series and interleave C independent problem instances, dropping the iteration bound C-fold at C times the per-instance latency — the only way under an FSM's next-state floor.

notes.name: 1011 Sequence Detector
notes.description: The canonical overlapping pattern detector, built twice: four Mealy states versus five Moore, with the one-hot invariant proved by induction and the binary encoding collapsing one flop into a shift register.

notes.name: Huffman Feedback Model
notes.description: The canonical asynchronous machine: one combinational network closed through its own lumped delays, so state exists without a clock — pays for it with an unknown settling order.
notes.spade_note: The loop y_i(t+D)=Y_i(t) is combinational feedback; `let y = f(x,y);` fails with "Use of undeclared name y". Nearest native structure is the same f() with y supplied by reg(clk), i.e. a synchronous Moore machine.

notes.name: Race-Free State Assignment
notes.description: Codes the flow table so every required transition is a Hamming-1 edge of the s-cube, killing critical races at the cost of extra state variables — a graph-embedding problem, not a counting one.
notes.spade_note: The encoding only means anything inside a fundamental-mode feedback machine, which has no Spade form. The same unit-distance idea in a clocked machine (Gray-coded state register) is expressible and should be the nearest-native block.
source_headings: ## Worked example: a critical race and its repair
### The excitation is not automatically hazard-free

notes.name: Asynchronous Cycle
notes.description: Chains several unstable states inside one input column so a distance-2 move happens one bit at a time — buys race freedom with transition time, and oscillates forever if the chain has no stable end.
notes.spade_note: A deliberately unstable combinational loop; Spade cannot close the feedback path at all, and the no-stable-state variant is a ring oscillator with no RTL meaning.

notes.name: Muller C-Element
notes.description: The rendezvous gate — output follows the inputs when they agree and holds when they disagree, giving asynchronous design its one state-holding primitive for free.
notes.spade_note: Y = ab + ay + by is majority with its own output fed back; `let y = a & b | a & y | b & y;` fails with "Use of undeclared name y". Named explicitly in the plan as not-expressible.

notes.name: Muller Pipeline
notes.description: A chain of C-elements where a stage advances only when its predecessor is full and its successor has emptied — correct for any gate delay, no matched delays anywhere, at the price of half the stages being bubbles.
notes.spade_note: Built entirely from C-elements, which are combinational feedback. A clocked valid/ready elastic pipeline is the nearest native structure and compiles.

notes.name: Micropipeline
notes.description: Sutherland's Muller pipeline with capture-pass latches hung off each C-element, turning transition-signalled events into a real datapath stage.
notes.spade_note: Control is a C-element chain and the storage is event-sensitive (double-edge / capture-pass), neither of which Spade has — `reg(clk)` is single-edge only.

notes.name: Bundled-Data Interface
notes.description: Keeps an ordinary single-rail datapath and adds req/ack plus one matched delay line — the synchronous period constraint made local to one stage, so only the stages that run pay it.
notes.spade_note: The controller is clockless state-holding logic and correctness rests on a physical matched delay; a clocked req/ack FSM compiles and is the nearest native structure.

notes.name: Four-Phase Handshake
notes.description: Return-to-zero level signalling — req up, ack up, req down, ack down — so latch control is literally a wire, paid for with two round trips per datum.
notes.spade_note: Level-sensitive handshake control is combinational feedback (C-element or cross-coupled). A clocked four-phase FSM compiles and should be shown instead.

notes.name: Two-Phase Handshake
notes.description: Every transition is an event, halving wire toggles on long links — wins when the wire dominates and loses when the event-sensitive storage it forces does.
notes.spade_note: Requires event-sensitive (double-edge / XOR-toggle) storage with no clock; Spade's `reg(clk)` is single-edge. A clocked toggle-encoded req/ack pair is the nearest native structure.

notes.name: Dual-Rail Encoding
notes.description: Two wires per bit with a spacer code, so validity announces itself and every timing assumption disappears — costs 2k wires, double area, and data-independent switching that is terrible for power and excellent against side channels.

notes.name: 1-of-4 Encoding
notes.description: Carries two bits on four wires with exactly one wire toggling per symbol — same wire count as dual-rail, half the transitions.

notes.name: Completion Detection Tree
notes.description: ORs each dual-rail pair and trees the results, so the datapath tells you when it is finished instead of a clock guessing — and puts that tree on the critical path.
notes.spade_note: The AND-of-ORs form is pure combinational logic and compiles. The four-phase variant that swaps ANDs for C-elements is not expressible; say so in the note.

notes.name: Matched Delay Line
notes.description: A delay longer than the datapath it shadows, so a bundled-data request never outruns its data — the one thing in the flow you must build, and the one thing synthesis will delete.
notes.spade_note: Purely a timing element with the identity logic function; it exists as a CARRY4/LUT-chain instantiation plus placement and DONT_TOUCH constraints, and has no RTL expression — an inverter chain written in Spade collapses to a wire.

notes.name: Mutual Exclusion Element
notes.description: Grants exactly one of two competing requests and holds the grant until release, filtering the metastability that any genuinely unclocked arbitration must contain somewhere.
notes.spade_note: Cross-coupled NANDs plus an analog metastability filter — combinational feedback, and the filter is not even digital.

notes.name: Asynchronous FIFO
notes.description: Gray-coded read and write pointers crossing into the other clock domain through synchronisers — race-free unit-distance assignment doing real work, and the only piece of this topic an FPGA actually runs.

notes.name: Signed Fixed-Point Format
notes.description: Negates the weight of the MSB only, so one integer adder serves signed and unsigned alike — at the cost of an asymmetric range with no opposite for -2^m.
source_headings: ### Two's complement as an algebraic object

notes.name: Two's Complement Negator
notes.description: Negation as a row of inverters plus an increment, where the increment is free because it rides the consuming adder's carry-in.
source_headings: ### Two's complement as an algebraic object

notes.name: Sign-Magnitude to Two's Complement Converter
notes.description: One conditional negate in each direction — an XOR row plus an increment gated by the sign bit — and the one input value, -2^(w-1), on which the reverse direction cannot work.
source_headings: ### Two's complement as an algebraic object

notes.name: Sign Extension
notes.description: Widening a signed word for free: replicate the sign bit left, pad zeros right — fanout of one wire, no gates, no delay.

notes.name: Fixed-Point Format Narrowing
notes.description: Splits the unavoidable loss of bits into two independent failure modes — catastrophic overflow at the MSB, quantifiable rounding at the LSB — and makes l the cursor of the area-versus-accuracy trade.
source_headings: ### Narrowing: overflow at the top, rounding at the bottom

notes.name: Carry-Free Signed-Digit Adder
notes.description: Addition in O(1) instead of O(w): rewrite every column sum into an anticipated-carry word and a residue word, then add the two digit-parallel with no propagation at all.

notes.name: IEEE 754 Format
notes.description: Sign, biased exponent and a normalised significand whose leading 1 is never stored — a free bit of precision, unique representations, and 2^277 of dynamic range on 32 bits.

notes.name: Nfloat Format
notes.description: Normals only, with all four special cases in an explicit 2-bit exn field: two bits more than IEEE 754, one extra binade at each end, and no subnormal logic in any operator of the pipeline.
source_headings: ### Nfloat: the simplification for application-specific hardware

notes.name: LNS Multiplier
notes.description: Multiply, divide, square and square root as one adder, one subtractor, one left shift and one right shift on the logarithm — all four exact, O(w) area against O(w^2) for a fixed-point multiplier.

notes.name: LNS Adder
notes.description: Addition turns transcendental: one subtractor, one evaluation of log2(1 + 2^r) over the whole word, one adder — and the table for it has 2^(wE+wF) entries, which is why LNS lives only in small formats.

notes.name: Truncation Unit
notes.description: Free rounding — the discarded bits are simply not routed — at the cost of a one-signed error under 1 ulp whose mean drifts by -u/2 per site.

notes.name: Round-to-Nearest Ties-Up
notes.description: Halves the worst-case error to 1/2 ulp for the price of one added constant 2^(l-1), and costs nothing at all when that constant can be absorbed into a bit heap or a spare carry-in.
source_headings: ## Rounding and Overflow in Fixed-Point Libraries

notes.name: Round-to-Nearest Ties-to-Even
notes.description: The IEEE 754 default: same 1/2 ulp bound as ties-up but unbiased and symmetric about zero, paid for with explicit tie detection and an LSB force.

notes.name: Directed Rounding Unit
notes.description: Round toward zero, away from zero, or toward +inf — the only modes that give provably one-signed interval bounds, and the only ones that are both less accurate and more expensive than round-to-nearest.
source_headings: ## Rounding and Overflow in Fixed-Point Libraries

notes.name: Saturating Overflow Unit
notes.description: Clamps out-of-range results to the extreme representable value instead of wrapping them, buying signal-processing sanity for one comparator and one multiplexer per operation.
source_headings: ## Rounding and Overflow in Fixed-Point Libraries

notes.name: Half-Unit Biased Format
notes.description: An implicit trailing 1 at weight 2^(l-1) makes negation a bitwise inversion and makes rounding-to-nearest exactly free, at the price of never representing zero.

notes.name: Faithful Operator
notes.description: The generic accuracy-driven architecture: an approximate datapath carrying g guard bits followed by one final rounding, sized so the whole block errs by strictly less than 1 ulp of its output.
source_headings: ## Last-Bit Accuracy vs. Rounding to the Nearest
## Using the Format to Specify the Accuracy

notes.name: Faithful Multiplier by Pi
notes.description: The chapter's whole method closed on one concrete operator: approximate pi to l_ext bits, multiply, truncate, round once — and the budget says g=2 guard bits, no more.
source_headings: ## Rounding to the Nearest When an Approximation Is Involved

notes.name: Correctly-Rounded Product Table
notes.description: A ROM holding every correctly-rounded product, which exists only because pi is transcendental so no product ever lands on a tie — the finite architecture the multiplier cannot match.
source_headings: ## Rounding to the Nearest When an Approximation Is Involved

notes.name: Error Analysis
notes.description: Telescoping a computation through virtual intermediate values until every term is boundable, then applying the triangle inequality exactly once at the end.
notes.spade_note: A proof method, not a structure; the architecture it analyses lives in Faithful Operator.

notes.name: Lookup-Tables
notes.description: A 2^alpha-bit SRAM read through a 2^alpha:1 multiplexer — realizes ANY Boolean function of alpha inputs, which is why FPGA area is counted in LUTs and not in gates.
source_headings: ## Shannon expansion, and why a $k$-LUT is universal

notes.name: Basic Logic Element
notes.description: The minimal FPGA cell: one LUT plus an optional flip-flop selected by a config bit — free pipelining, because an unused FF is wasted silicon rather than saved area.
source_headings: ## Comparison of BLEs across commercial families

notes.name: Fracturable LUT
notes.description: One LUT6 split into two LUT5s over shared inputs by Boole's expansion — twice the logic per cell, but only when both halves have the same support set.
source_headings: ## Shannon expansion, and why a $k$-LUT is universal

notes.name: AMD BLE
notes.description: Three generations of the Xilinx/AMD logic element — Virtex-4 LUT4 with a dedicated AND, Virtex-5/7/UltraScale fracturable LUT6 with two FFs, Versal four LUT4s with cascade routing — and what changed in each.
source_headings: ## Comparison of BLEs across commercial families

notes.name: Intel ALM
notes.description: Intel's half-ALM: one LUT4, two LUT3s, a HARDENED full adder and two FFs — the adder costs no LUT, so both LUT layers stay free to feed it.
source_headings: ## Comparison of BLEs across commercial families

notes.name: Fast Carry Chain
notes.description: A dedicated wire handing one carry bit to the neighbouring BLE, bypassing the switch matrix: a carry crosses a bit 38x faster than it enters one, so below 32 bits carry propagation is not worth optimizing.
source_headings: ## Worked example — 8-bit addition on the fast carry chain

notes.name: DSP Blocks
notes.description: Hard multiplier wrapped in an optional pre-adder and post-adder computing R = (X0+X1)*Y+Z — a free multiplier until you run out, then the most expensive resource on the chip.
source_headings: ## Trade-off: three ways to compute the same small function

notes.name: Three-Multiplication Complex Product
notes.description: Gauss's trick mapped onto a DSP's pre- and post-adders: 3 multiplications and 5 additions instead of 4 and 2, because the adders are already sitting there unused.

notes.name: Distributed Memory
notes.description: A SLICEM LUT turned inside out: its SRAM cells become writable FFs with a one-hot write decoder, giving a simple dual-port 64x1 (or 2x 32x1) RAM per LUT6 — the cheapest ROM on the chip.

notes.name: Shift Register LUT
notes.description: The SLICEM's other mode: the 32 FFs chained instead of addressed, giving an addressable 32-deep delay line in one LUT5 — and a way to rewrite a LUT's contents through one wire in 32 cycles.

notes.name: Block Memory
notes.description: Dedicated 36 kbit (AMD) / 20 kbit (Intel) dual-port RAM tiles with configurable depth-width trade-off — full clock rate but several cycles per access, so a throughput resource, never a latency one.
source_headings: ## Trade-off: three ways to compute the same small function

notes.name: Full Adder
notes.description: The one-digit column of paper-and-pencil addition: sum is XOR of three bits, carry is their majority — the cell every other adder in the vault is made of.

notes.name: Half Adder
notes.description: Full adder with one input known zero: XOR plus AND. Shaves the LSB cell of any adder with c0=0 and rewrites X+Y as S+C in one layer.

notes.name: RCA, Ripple-Carry Adder
notes.description: w full adders chained carry-to-carry: minimal area, O(w) latency, and the baseline delay every fast adder is trying to beat.

notes.name: Saturating Adder
notes.description: Modulo-2^w interface plus one multiplexer on c_out that substitutes the maximal representable value — clipping instead of wraparound, which is what signal processing needs.

notes.name: Two's Complement Adder/Subtractor
notes.description: One XOR per bit plus a sub signal on the carry-in turns any adder into S = X + (-1)^sub Y at zero delay cost; carries the signed/unsigned overflow test with it.

notes.name: CSA, Carry-Save Adder
notes.description: A row of full adders that keeps its carries instead of rippling them: three vectors in, two out, delay independent of w — the core trick of every multiplier and divider.

notes.name: High-Radix Carry-Save Adder
notes.description: Carry-save with alpha-bit carry propagation inside each group: fewer redundant bits to register, longer critical path — a clean area/speed knob on the redundancy.

notes.name: Switched Ripple-Carry Adder
notes.description: RCA topology where a GKP block steers fast switches that pass, pull down or pull up the carry — Zuse's Z3 relay adder, and exactly what an FPGA carry chain is.

notes.name: Carry-Select Adder
notes.description: Split into m-bit groups, compute both carry-in answers in parallel, select when the carry arrives: doubles the area to replace m carry stages with one mux delay.

notes.name: Conditional-Sum Adder
notes.description: Carry-select applied to itself — a mux tree instead of a mux chain gives the first O(log w) adder at linear area, paid for with w/2 fan-out on the top select.

notes.name: CLA, Carry-Lookahead Adder
notes.description: Unroll the carry recurrence into two levels of logic — AND rank into a wide OR — then cap the group at m=4 because fan-in, not depth, is what actually costs.

notes.name: Hierarchical Carry-Lookahead Adder
notes.description: Each CLA-m block also emits its group generate and propagate for free, so the blocks compose in a radix-m tree: log_m(w) levels of fat nodes, and the prefix formulation one paragraph early.

notes.name: Parallel Prefix Adders
notes.description: All carries are the prefixes of one associative reduction, so any prefix graph is correct by construction — correctness is free and only depth, node count, fan-out and wire tracks differ.
source_headings: ## Carry propagation as a prefix problem
### The prefix operator and its associativity

notes.name: Kogge-Stone Tree
notes.description: Every output gets its own balanced tree shifted by one: minimum depth log2(w) with fan-out capped at 2, paid for in w*log2(w) nodes and a layout dominated by wire tracks.

notes.name: Brent-Kung Tree
notes.description: Reduction tree up, inverse distribution tree down: the fewest nodes and the lightest, most regular wiring, at one extra stage and a constant fan-out of 3.

notes.name: Sklansky Tree
notes.description: Recursive halving on the outputs: minimum depth with only (w/2)log2(w) nodes, and the bill arrives as fan-out w/2 on every block midpoint.

notes.name: Compound Adder
notes.description: Only the bottom row of a prefix adder depends on c0, so duplicating that one linear row yields X+Y and X+Y+1 at once — the standard significand adder for floating-point rounding.

notes.name: Absolute Difference Operator
notes.description: One compound prefix tree over (X, ~Y) yields both X-Y and Y-X because Y-X = ~(X+~Y); a constant-time mux picks, and one NOR gives an equality flag cheaper than a comparator.

notes.name: Compound Triple Sum
notes.description: A half-adder row collapses position 0 to a single bit, so one compound adder on the upper bits plus three muxes delivers X+Y, X+Y+1 and X+Y+2 with no second prefix tree.

notes.name: FPGA Hard Carry Chain Adder
notes.description: The mux form of the full adder hardened into the BLE: 0.015 ns per bit on dedicated routing, 38x faster than the LUT it sits in — which is why fast adder trees lose on FPGA below 256 bits.

notes.name: LUT-Merged Adder
notes.description: An adder barely uses the LUT in front of it, so arbitrary logic rides along for free: a third addend, a sub select, a source mux, a KCM table or partial products, at zero extra resources.
source_headings: ### Merging extra functionality into an adder

notes.name: Ternary Adders on FPGAs
notes.description: Spend the idle LUT layer on a carry-save row and let the hard chain collapse it: X+Y+Z in the same ALM count as a binary adder on Intel shared-arithmetic mode, up to 50 percent slower on AMD.

notes.name: Sign-Configurable Adder/Subtractor
notes.description: Negating both inputs needs a constant +2 and there is only one carry-in, so build it on the ternary structure: XOR of the two sub bits gives the +1, AND gives the +2 — the SAD kernel.

notes.name: Pipelined Ripple-Carry Adder
notes.description: On FPGA an unused flip-flop is wasted, not saved, so cut the RCA into m-bit stages; the DNP10 variant puts real adders in early stages to halve the balancing registers.

notes.name: AAM Carry-Select Adder
notes.description: Carry-select whose selection is a ripple-carry adder on the fast chain instead of a mux tree: c_i = c_i^0 OR (~s_i AND c_i^1) fits one LUT5 per bit and gives single-cycle 256+ bit adders.

notes.name: Equality Comparator
notes.description: Decides X=Y with w XNORs and a balanced AND tree, log-depth and the only predicate that gets cheaper when you ask for less.

notes.name: Magnitude Comparator
notes.description: X<Y as the negated carry-out of X+~Y+1: one adder's leftmost carry path, every sum bit discarded.

notes.name: Two's-Complement Comparator
notes.description: Signed comparison for free: exchange the two MSBs and run the unsigned comparator; format alignment is zero-padding, also free.

notes.name: Binary Tree Comparator
notes.description: Divide-and-conquer comparison carrying a (greater, equal) pair per edge — the same prefix operator as the adder's (g,p), at log-depth with no leaf logic.

notes.name: Fast Carry Chain Comparator
notes.description: Two aligned 2-bit chunks per BLE feed a synthetic subtraction on the dedicated carry chain: w/2 LUTs for X<Y, the area optimum and the latency optimum to 64 bits.
source_headings: ## Worked example: 16-bit comparison against a constant

notes.name: Two-Level Fast Carry Comparator
notes.description: Parallel k-bit chunk comparisons re-encoded as two synthetic integers and compared again on a second carry chain: two chains of sqrt(w) instead of one of w/2, at strictly worse area.
source_headings: ### The two-level tree of fast carry logic

notes.name: Constant Comparator
notes.description: Freezing Y collapses every leaf to a wire or an inverter, so a LUT sees alpha bits of X alone — chunk width, LUT count and chain depth all improve by the same factor.
source_headings: ## Worked example: 16-bit comparison against a constant

notes.name: Bit Heaps
notes.description: One canonical form — a multiset of weighted bits — that swallows partial products, table outputs, sign-extension and rounding constants alike, so every operator reduces to one summation problem; costs you the word-level structure that made resource sharing obvious.
source_headings: ### A Multiplier as a Compressor Tree
### From Bit Arrays to Bit Heaps
### Bit Heaps as the Portable Substrate

notes.name: Merged Multiply-Accumulate
notes.description: Folds XY+A into the product's own heap for one extra row and at most one extra compression level, instead of a separate n-bit adder behind the multiplier costing n delay or n log n area.
source_headings: ### From Bit Arrays to Bit Heaps

notes.name: Constant-One Sign Extension
notes.description: Replaces the replicated sign bit of every signed summand with one complemented bit plus a compile-time constant, so the whole heap's signedness collapses to a single row of constant ones and some inverters instead of one fanout tree per summand.

notes.name: Single-Heap Polynomial Evaluation
notes.description: Expands a polynomial such as X−X³/6 directly into one heap using x^k=x and 2·2^p a = 2^(p+1) a, beating two chained multipliers on area for w<14 and always on latency because it is one compression instead of two; the 1/3 becomes an infinite tail of weighted bits, which truncation handles anyway.

notes.name: Truncated Bit Heap
notes.description: Two parameters (ℓ_ext, t) delete the cheapest bits from the right of an exact heap while staying faithful to 2^ℓ, and a correction constant C=2^(ℓ−1)−2^(ℓ_ext) recentres the one-signed error on zero, doubling how much you may drop; costs you a worst-case bound that can be pessimistic when the heap holds both x and x̄.
source_headings: ### Truncating a Bit Heap for Last-Bit Accuracy

notes.name: Compressor Trees
notes.description: Any heap becomes a height-2 heap in Θ(log_1.5 h) combinational levels with no carry propagation inside the tree — only the final adder propagates; costs wide irregular interconnect and a final adder whose length the schedule decides.
source_headings: ### A Multiplier as a Compressor Tree

notes.name: Dadda Tree
notes.description: Schedules full adders as late as possible against the sequence m_l=⌊1.5·m_(l−1)⌋, which minimises FA and HA count; costs the longest final adder (14 bits on the 8×8 example), the widest interconnect and the most flip-flops if pipelined.

notes.name: Reduced Area Compressor Tree
notes.description: Bickerstaff's as-soon-as-possible schedule: maximum full adders per column every level, half adders only to respect the Dadda bound or to start carry propagation early — same stage count as Dadda, more cells, but a 10-bit final adder instead of 14 and far fewer flip-flops when pipelined.

notes.name: Wallace Tree
notes.description: The classic as-soon-as-possible full-adder schedule: compress every column the moment three bits exist, trading extra cells for the shallowest tree — the historical ASAP pole that Reduced Area occupies in this book.

notes.name: Parallel Counter
notes.description: A (p;q) cell turns a column of p bits into a row of q=⌈log2(p+1)⌉ bits; compression per output bit peaks at p=2^q−1, giving (7;3) and (15;4), but it is dead weight once the heap is shorter than p and only wins if hand-optimised below gate level.

notes.name: 4:2 Compressor
notes.description: Two full adders per cell plus one lateral k_i signal to the neighbour: 4n+1 bits into 2n+1 with no carry propagation, so unlike a counter it stays usable down to the last compression stage; only pays on ASIC if the cell is hand-optimised at gate or transistor level.

notes.name: Carry-Chain 4:2 Compressor
notes.description: The FPGA variant that deliberately keeps the fast carry chain instead of avoiding it, saving the carry as an extra output row: efficiency 2−1/k, beating the ternary adder at much shorter delay.

notes.name: Generalized Parallel Counter
notes.description: A (p_(n−1),…,p_0;q) cell absorbing inputs of different weights at once; a 6-input LUT tabulates any GPC under six inputs outright and the fast carry chain fits a (1,3,2,5;5) into one AMD slice at efficiency 1.5 — which is why the plain full adder is the worst compressor on FPGA.

notes.name: Efficiency-Driven Compression Heuristic
notes.description: Orders a library by E=δ/k and greedily places the best effective-efficiency compressor per column per stage, with a pseudo (1;1) GPC guaranteeing progress; runs in seconds on 16 384-bit heaps at a linear 0.55 LUT6 per compressed bit, usually one stage worse than optimal.

notes.name: Pipelined Compressor Tree
notes.description: Registers between compression stages turn the free (1;1) pseudo GPC into a flip-flop priced at 0.5 LUT6, which flips the objective toward compressing early — and is why Reduced Area beats Dadda the moment the tree is pipelined.

notes.name: Split Final Adder
notes.description: Bits out of a triangular heap arrive Gaussian-like — LSBs and MSBs first, middle last — so a uniform fast adder is wasted: ripple-carry on the early LSBs, a prefix adder across the late middle, carry-select on MSBs whose carry-in arrives last. Truncation flattens the profile and pipelining removes it.

notes.name: Unsigned Array Multiplier
notes.description: Schoolbook radix-2 partial products: one AND gate per bit pair, a w_X x w_Y rectangle dropped into a bit heap — the baseline every other multiplier is measured against.
source_headings: ## Partial product generation and sign management

notes.name: Baugh-Wooley Multiplier
notes.description: Two's-complement radix-2 array: sign-extend every row, negate the top row, then collapse all the sign-extension runs into a handful of constant bits — signedness for almost free.

notes.name: Booth's Algorithm
notes.description: Modified radix-4 recoding into the redundant digit set {-2..2}: halves the partial-product rows for the price of an OR and an XOR per bit, and never needs 3Y.

notes.name: Bewick Radix-8 Multiplier
notes.description: Keeps the awkward 3Y/5Y/7Y multiples of a high-radix recoding in carry-save form built from small ripple-carry adders — one carry bit per k sum bits instead of a full extra row.

notes.name: Unsigned DSP Multiplier Packing
notes.description: Two small unsigned multiplications sharing an operand out of one 18x27 DSP: concatenate A and B with w_P zeros between them, slice the two products back out of R. No extra adder.

notes.name: Signed DSP Multiplier Packing
notes.description: Same DSP-sharing trick for signed operands: the DSP pre-adder builds A_sign-extended + 2^k B, and the upper product is corrected by adding the single precomputed sign bit of the lower one.

notes.name: Multiplier Tiling
notes.description: Builds a large multiplier by covering the w_X x w_Y partial-product rectangle with sub-multipliers exactly once; each tile's output is shifted by its lower-right corner and dropped into the compressor tree.
source_headings: ### Multiplier construction as a tiling problem

notes.name: LUT-Based Multiplier Tiles
notes.description: Small multipliers tabulated straight into LUT6s — 1x1, 1x2, 3x3, and the 2x3 that exploits LUT6-as-two-LUT5 to beat 3x3 on efficiency. The 1x1 exists only to guarantee a tiling always closes.
source_headings: ### Multiplier construction as a tiling problem

notes.name: Carry-Chain Multiplier Tile
notes.description: A Baugh-Wooley row mapped onto an FPGA slice: two bit-products per LUT summed directly by the fast carry chain, giving a 2xk tile whose efficiency passes every LUT-only tile at k=6 and tends to 1.29.
source_headings: ### Multiplier construction as a tiling problem

notes.name: DSP Super-Tile
notes.description: Two 17x24 DSP blocks chained through the dedicated post-adder routing — legal only at relative shifts of 0 or 17 bits — doubling LUT efficiency at the cost of one pipeline stage.
source_headings: ### Multiplier construction as a tiling problem

notes.name: Correctly Rounded Multiplier
notes.description: Round-to-nearest-ties-up for the price of one constant bit: inject a 1 at position l_P - 1 into the exact multiplier's bit heap and truncate the compressed result at l_P.

notes.name: Truncated Multipliers
notes.description: Never compute the low partial products at all: keep g guard columns below l_P, drop the rest, compensate with a constant, and stay faithful. Booth recoding buys one extra truncated column.

notes.name: Karatsuba
notes.description: Recovers the middle column of a two-part split by subtraction instead of multiplication: three sub-multipliers instead of four, paid for with two pre-additions on the critical path.

notes.name: Subtractive Karatsuba
notes.description: Same three-multiplier structure with pre-subtractions instead of pre-additions: the extra bit becomes a sign bit, so natively-signed DSP multipliers stop wasting theirs on a forced zero.

notes.name: K-Part Karatsuba Splitting
notes.description: Split both operands into K chunks and apply the pairing identity to every same-weight pair, reusing each diagonal sub-product more than once: saves the triangle of K(K-1)/2 multiplications.

notes.name: Recursive Karatsuba
notes.description: Apply the two-part split to the sub-multipliers themselves — nine small multipliers for 4w x 4w against ten for flat 4-part splitting, at the price of two pre-additions in sequence.

notes.name: Rectangular Karatsuba
notes.description: Pairs any two same-weight tiles anywhere on the rectangle, so DSP blocks can be used as 16x24 rather than 17x17; gcd(w_X,w_Y) sets the smallest pattern, and pre-adders become shareable.

notes.name: Restoring Division
notes.description: Cheapest divider there is — one subtractor and one mux per quotient bit — at w_Q cycles of latency, each a full carry propagation followed by the sign bit and the mux.

notes.name: Non-Restoring Division
notes.description: Removes the restore multiplexer by letting the remainder go negative — one add/sub per digit, controlled by the previous remainder's sign bit, paid for with one correction iteration.

notes.name: SRT Division
notes.description: Redundant digit set turns quotient digit selection into a small table read — radix-4 with digits -2..2 needs only a mux, a shift and an add/sub, packing into one row of 6-LUTs.
source_headings: ## Redundant Digit Sets and the Selection-Interval Overlap

notes.name: Radix-4 Maximally Redundant Divider
notes.description: The gamma=3 SRT variant: full selection-interval overlap shrinks the table to 4+1 input bits, but the digit set now needs 3D, a fourth mux input that breaks the single-LUT-row packing.

notes.name: Quotient Digit Selection Table
notes.description: The combinational block that reads 6 bits of the shifted remainder and 3 bits of the divisor and returns a signed digit — and the one border cell whose mislabelling was the Pentium FDIV bug.
source_headings: ## Redundant Digit Sets and the Selection-Interval Overlap

notes.name: Comparison-Based Digit Selection
notes.description: Selects the digit by comparing the shifted remainder in parallel against precomputed divisor multiples in the overlap regions — the only route to high-radix division of arbitrary integers, at two sequential carry propagations.

notes.name: Divisor Prescaling
notes.description: Two muxes and one adder push D into [0.984, 1.125] so digit selection collapses to rounding the shifted remainder to the nearest integer — enabling very high radices, at duplicated scaling hardware and a wider iteration datapath.

notes.name: On-the-Fly Quotient Conversion
notes.description: Converts the signed-digit quotient to binary using concatenation only, by carrying a pre-decremented copy alongside it — kills the final carry-propagate subtraction for two muxes and two registers per stage.

notes.name: Carry-Save Partial Remainder
notes.description: Keeps R_i in carry-save so the iteration has no carry propagation at all — the bill arrives at digit selection, where the ignored truncated carry eats 2^t/D off the selection-interval overlap.

notes.name: Radix-64 Speculative Divider
notes.description: Three radix-4 steps per cycle with carry-save remainder, strong prescaling, and every possible next remainder computed speculatively while the digit is chosen — the lowest-latency double-precision divider in the book, bought entirely with area.

notes.name: Division by Reciprocal
notes.description: Approximate 1/D then multiply by X — one table-or-polynomial block and one truncated multiplier, faithful only, and only usable when D is bounded away from zero.

notes.name: Reciprocal Seed Table
notes.description: A ROM on the truncated leading bits of D returning R_0 = floor(1/(D_0 + 2^lT)), which forces R_0 <= 1/D and 1/2 <= R_0 < 1 — the initial approximation every multiplicative divider starts from.

notes.name: Newton-Raphson Reciprocal
notes.description: r_{i+1} = 2r_i - D r_i^2 doubles the correct bits per step and is self-correcting because e_i is re-measured against D — one exact squarer then one truncated multiplier in sequence, datapath doubling every step.

notes.name: Quadratic Series Divider
notes.description: Same quadratic convergence as Newton-Raphson but the squarer and the multiplier run in parallel instead of in sequence — shorter step, and the E datapath shrinks each iteration instead of growing.

notes.name: Goldschmidt Division
notes.description: Two coupled recurrences driving the denominator to 1, with both multiplications issuing in the same cycle — pipelines beautifully, but the numerator error is never re-measured so it accumulates and must be paid for in guard bits.

notes.name: Halley Reciprocal Iteration
notes.description: Order-2 Householder: x_i(1 + e_i + e_i^2) triples the precision of the seed per step for one squarer and two multipliers, filling the gap between one and two quadratic steps.

notes.name: VFloat Ad Hoc Series Divider
notes.description: Splits D = D_H + D_L and tabulates 1/D_H^2 so the table read and the first multiplication run in parallel — attractive only at small precisions where both multipliers fit in DSP blocks.

notes.name: Newton-Raphson Square Root
notes.description: Zeroing 1/x^2 - X gives s_{i+1} = s_i(3 - s_i^2 X)/2, converging to the inverse square root without a division — one squarer and two multipliers per step, faithful only.

notes.name: Exact Full Shifter
notes.description: Stack of w_S mux rows shifting by 2^i, output widened to w_X+S_max so no input bit is ever lost; LSB-first stage order minimises summed mux width and overlaps with the adder producing S.
source_headings: Derivation: a shift is a binary power of one operator
Architecture of an Exact Full Shifter

notes.name: Barrel Shifters
notes.description: The w_X=w_R case: every stage the same width, w_X*ceil(log2(S_max+1)) 1-bit muxes at log depth, uniform fanout on every s_i — the ALU shifter, necessarily truncated.

notes.name: Truncated Shifter
notes.description: Any shifter with w_R < w_X+S_max: cheaper than an exact full shifter because it never builds the hardware feeding bits doomed to be discarded, at the price of up to 1 ulp unless a sticky bit is kept.
source_headings: Parameters of a Generic Shifter Generator
Architecture of an Exact Full Shifter

notes.name: Shifter with Sticky Bit Computation
notes.description: Barrel shifter in reversed (largest-shift-first) stage order that ORs each stage's discarded bits in place; turns an exact full shifter plus wide OR into a same-width barrel shifter, measured 20% less area and 5% less delay in a binary32 adder.
source_headings: Barrel Shifter with Early Sticky-Bit Computation

notes.name: Bidirectional Shifter
notes.description: A shifter taking a direction bit or signed S; the book's advice is not to build one — bias S by a constant offset and use a unidirectional shifter instead, which is free in a floating-point context because the offset merges into the exponent bias.
source_headings: Parameters of a Generic Shifter Generator

notes.name: One-Hot Shifter
notes.description: One (S_max+1):1 mux per output bit driven by a one-hot decode of S: same asymptotic depth as a barrel shifter but quadratic area and fanout S_max on every input bit, so it loses above trivial widths.

notes.name: Shift by Multiplier
notes.description: A left shift is a multiply by 2^S, so one-hot encode S in logic and feed a DSP block; faster and cheaper than a logic shifter whenever a DSP is idle, as in some AMD floating-point adder cores.

notes.name: Sporadic Shifter
notes.description: When only a discrete subset of shift distances is ever needed, the multiplexer network is optimised against that set instead of against the whole range [0,S_max].

notes.name: Leading Zero Counters
notes.description: The naive recursive LZC: one wide NOR per level emits count bit c_k and selects between the upper and lower halves; area linear in w_X but delay k(k+1)/2, i.e. O(log^2 w_X) — still the right choice on FPGAs and the only one that fuses with a shifter.

notes.name: Leading Bit Counter
notes.description: LZC generalised with a runtime input b naming the bit value to count (the leading one counter is the b=1 case); one extra XOR layer, paid for with the fanout of b — which is why the book keeps LZC, LOC and LBC as three components.

notes.name: Oklobdzija LZC Tree
notes.description: Balanced binary tree over the associative operator (z,C): LZC(k+1) merges two LZC(k) with z=z_L AND z_R and a concatenation-select; O(log w_X) delay for about 2*w_X muxes, but the select drives a whole k-bit mux so fanout must be charged to the delay.

notes.name: Monotonic String Leading Zero Counter
notes.description: Prefix-OR the input into a thermometer code, AND it with its own negated one-bit shift to get a one-hot marker, then read each count bit off a w_X/2-wide OR; log depth with fanout limited to 2, and the form that generalises to LOC, LBC and anticipation.

notes.name: Leading Zero Anticipation
notes.description: Approximates the leading-zero count of a sum directly from the addends, running in parallel with the addition so the LZC leaves the floating-point adder's critical path entirely.

notes.name: Normalizers
notes.description: LZC wired to a left shifter: outputs the normalized word R and the count C, turning a fixed-point number into a significand plus exponent. Pipelinable and constant-latency, but two full latencies in series.

notes.name: Fused Normalizer
notes.description: Merges the naive LZC into the shifter: each level NORs its top 2^j bits, emits c_j and immediately shifts under it, so the MSB-first count bits are consumed as they are produced. O(w_X log w_X) area, and near log w_X delay on FPGA — but no place to do arithmetic on the count, so not for IEEE-754.

notes.name: Sequential Normalizer
notes.description: A state machine that shifts left one bit per cycle while the MSB is zero, counting as it goes; the cheapest normalizer in existence and the only one with variable latency, so it cannot be pipelined.

notes.name: Exponent Difference and Swap Unit
notes.description: Produces |Ex-Ey| and orders the operands so Ex>=Ey, in two subtractors and a mux layer instead of a subtract-compare-subtract chain; on FPGAs the comparison is done on the whole exponent-fraction concatenation so the significand block never needs an absolute value.

notes.name: Floating-Point Adder
notes.description: Alignment shifter, significand adder, LZC+normalizer and rounding adder in series: the smallest thing that adds two floats to round-to-nearest ties-away, at the price of five log-depth blocks on one critical path.
source_headings: ## Why addition is the hard one
## Worked example: an 8-bit addition with a worst-case alignment

notes.name: Dual-Path Floating-Point Adder
notes.description: Splits the adder on the observation that a large alignment shift and a large normalization shift are mutually exclusive, cutting five slow blocks to two per path for one extra significand adder and one output mux.
source_headings: ### Dual-path architectures and other speculative techniques

notes.name: Leading Zero Anticipator
notes.description: Predicts the leading zero count from the two operands in parallel with the subtraction rather than measuring it on the result, moving the LZC off the near path's critical path for the cost of a one-bit correction mux.
source_headings: ### Dual-path architectures and other speculative techniques

notes.name: Speculative Floating-Point Adder
notes.description: Lutz's 1-cycle double-precision adder: compute all four near-path differences, both far-path shifts and both rounding pre-additions while the exponents are still subtracting, then mux. Two 54-bit incrementers and seven 54-bit adders.
source_headings: ### Dual-path architectures and other speculative techniques

notes.name: Sticky Bit Generator
notes.description: The OR of everything shifted past the round bit — either a full shifter plus a wide OR tree, or generation folded into the shifter itself. Mandatory for directed rounding, and the bulk of an adder's IEEE 754 compliance cost.
source_headings: ### From baseline adder to IEEE 754 compliance

notes.name: Floating-Point Rounding Adder
notes.description: Adds a single 1 at the LSB of the concatenated exponent and fraction so that a fraction overflow carries straight into the exponent field and zeroes the fraction for free — the reason a biased exponent costs nothing.
source_headings: ### From baseline adder to IEEE 754 compliance

notes.name: Floating-Point Exception Handling
notes.description: The unpack/pack logic that decodes NaN, infinity, zero and subnormal codes on the way in and re-encodes overflow and underflow from a wE+2-bit exponent on the way out; a flat layer of gates around every operator in the chapter.

notes.name: Subnormal Normalization Unit
notes.description: Turns subnormal inputs into an internal normal format with a leading zero counter, one shifter and a 1-bit wider exponent — plus the cheaper trick of feeding the "is normal" bit in as the implicit bit and shifting only the result.
source_headings: ### From baseline adder to IEEE 754 compliance

notes.name: Floating-Point Multiplier
notes.description: Exponent add and significand multiply are independent, so normalization is a single mux over a statically known two-binade product range, and the exponent increment is a mux instead of a carry propagation.

notes.name: Faithful Floating-Point Multiplier
notes.description: Swap the exact significand multiplier for a truncated one faithful to ufix(1,-wF-1): the error budget closes at 1 ulp in both binades and the architecture is unchanged, for an appreciable area and delay saving.

notes.name: Injection Rounding
notes.description: Fuses the rounding adder into the multiplier by injecting the constant 2^(-wF-1) as one more bit-heap column, with a compound adder and a mux over the overflow bit covering the second binade. Two slow blocks become one.

notes.name: Floating-Point Divider
notes.description: A normalized divisor removes the singularity at zero, so all that is left is exponent management: the -1 for the possible left normalization is folded into the bias by replacing the LSB of E0 with the quotient's leading bit — a wire, not an adder.

notes.name: Correct Rounding from Faithful Quotient
notes.description: Buys the last ulp out of a faithful quotient one bit wider than the target: if the LSB is 0 it is already correctly rounded, otherwise a left-truncated multiplier decides the sign of the remainder. A whole multiply and a second rounding for one bit.
source_headings: ### Correct rounding out of a faithfully rounded quotient

notes.name: Floating-Point Square Root
notes.description: The easiest FP operator: never overflows, never underflows, and needs no rounding or normalization logic outside the sqrt block. Exponent halving is one addition because floor(E0/2) is a constant string of ones and the parity bit is the carry-in.

notes.name: Faithful Square Root Normalization Unit
notes.description: Fixes the single input value where a faithful square root may return 2.0, unrepresentable in the output format: widen MS by one bit and let its MSB mux between ES and a precomputed ES+1. One value, catastrophically wrong, invisible to random testing.

notes.name: Left-Truncated Squarer
notes.description: Decides the sign of S0^2 - X to lift a faithful square root to a correctly rounded one, computing only the bits of the square that can differ from X — the square-root transpose of the divider's left-truncated multiplier.
source_headings: ### Correct rounding out of faithful rounding

notes.name: Floating-Point Comparator
notes.description: Because the biased encoding makes the bit pattern order the numeric order (subnormals included), comparison is an integer comparator on the concatenated exponent and fraction plus a flat layer of NaN/zero/infinity logic.

notes.name: Incrementer
notes.description: An n-bit +1 built as a chain of half adders — one XOR2 and one AND2 per bit, roughly half an adder's gates, with the enable absorbed as carry-in and terminal count free as carry-out.
source_headings: ## The increment is an adder with one operand tied to 1

notes.name: Prefix Incrementer
notes.description: Lookahead increment where the carry prefix degenerates to a pure AND-prefix — log-depth carry, half the wires of the adder tree because the generate rail vanishes.
source_headings: ## The increment is an adder with one operand tied to 1

notes.name: Synchronous Counters
notes.description: One clock for the whole word: state valid after t_cq regardless of width, at the cost of putting the increment chain inside the clock period.

notes.name: Up-Down Counter
notes.description: One datapath both directions: XOR the direction bit into each toggle product, so bit i flips when all lower bits are 1 (up) or all 0 (down) — one literal per AND input, free on a LUT fabric.
source_headings: ## The increment is an adder with one operand tied to 1

notes.name: Asynchronous Counters
notes.description: Ripple chain of divide-by-twos with no increment logic at all — highest raw toggle rate and one flop on the clock tree, paid for with n·t_cq of invalid word and a decoded glitch at every edge.

notes.name: Cascaded Counter Chain
notes.description: Wide counters from k-bit slices: ripple-carry enable (ENT chained, depth linear in slices) versus parallel enable (constant depth, wide AND and high state fan-in per slice).

notes.name: Two-Stage Prescaled Counter
notes.description: Fast k-bit low half gates a slow (n-k)-bit high half, so the long carry chain gets 2^k periods to settle and f_max is set by the small slice alone.

notes.name: Modulo-N Counter
notes.description: Compare-and-clear: an equality match on N-1 drives a synchronous clear — costs a comparator in series with the increment, but the clear port is free on FPGA and Q runs 0..N-1 upward for addressing.

notes.name: Preload-and-Overflow Counter
notes.description: Load 2^n - N and count up so the wrap condition is the incrementer's own carry-out — the comparator disappears entirely, at the price of the load mux.

notes.name: Zero-Detect Down Counter
notes.description: The default timer: preload N-1, decrement, detect zero with an n-input NOR — terminal condition is the borrow-out, hardware is constant across every N, and N becomes a register value rather than a synthesis constant.

notes.name: Gray Counter
notes.description: Binary core with a registered Gray conversion beside it — exactly one bit in flight per step, so a sampled word is always either the old or the new count; the only cheap way to be correct across a clock domain.

notes.name: Gray Code Converter
notes.description: Binary to Gray is one row of XOR2 (g = b XOR b>>1); Gray to binary is a suffix-XOR, i.e. a prefix tree of depth log n — cheap one way, a tree the other.

notes.name: Fibonacci LFSR
notes.description: Shift register with tapped bits gathered into one wide XOR; a primitive polynomial gives period 2^n - 1 for n flops and |T|-1 gates, at the cost of a non-monotone count and a dead all-zeros state.

notes.name: Galois LFSR
notes.description: Same sequence, taps XORed into the shift path instead of gathered: next-state depth is one XOR2 for any width, so T_clk is within a gate of the flop's own toggle limit.

notes.name: De Bruijn Counter
notes.description: An LFSR with an all-zeros detect XNORed into the feedback, splicing the missing state into the cycle for a full period of 2^n — costs one (n-1)-input NOR.

notes.name: Ring Counter
notes.description: One-hot rotation: N flops for N states — hopeless density — but the decode of state k is the flop output itself, so zero decode logic, zero delay, structurally glitch-free; needs self-correcting feedback or a reset.

notes.name: Johnson Counter
notes.description: Twisted ring feeding back the complement: 2n states from n flops, one bit changing per step (so it is a Gray code), decoded by one 2-input gate per state — the 2-bit case is quadrature clock phases.

notes.name: Binary Shift-and-Add Constant Multiplier
notes.description: Turns a hard-coded coefficient into nz(C)-1 adders and free wiring, because every partial product is known at synthesis time.
source_headings: Derivation: from bit vector to addition graph

notes.name: CSD Constant Multiplier
notes.description: Collapses each run of ones in the coefficient into a single subtracter, capping the adder count at ceil((n+1)/2)-1 instead of n.
source_headings: ### Signed digits and the run-of-ones identity

notes.name: Minimum-Adder Constant Multiplier
notes.description: The provably fewest-adder graph for one coefficient, found by enumerating topologies offline and looking the constant up in a table.
source_headings: ### Minimal-adder constant multiplication by graph enumeration

notes.name: Ternary-Adder Constant Multiplier
notes.description: Uses the FPGA carry chain's free third input so that every constant up to 22 bits needs at most three adders, saving about a third of the resources.

notes.name: Minimum Full-Adder Constant Multiplier
notes.description: Picks among equal-adder-count graphs the one whose shifts and negative intermediates leave the most LSBs as bare wires — 16 FA cells instead of 25 for 49X.
source_headings: ### Minimizing logic resources instead of adder count

notes.name: Tabulated Constant Multiplier
notes.description: One LUT per output bit and one LUT of delay while the input fits the LUT's alpha inputs — unbeatable, and exponentially bad one bit past that.

notes.name: KCM, Table-Based Constant Multiplication
notes.description: Tabulates the product of alpha-bit input chunks and sums them, giving cost linear in input width and flat in the constant's bit pattern.

notes.name: Tabulated Perfectly Rounded Constant Multiplier
notes.description: Stores the offline-rounded product of a real constant so exactly one rounding happens — the half-ulp reference every other real-constant technique is measured against.

notes.name: Faithful Shift-and-Add Real Constant Multiplier
notes.description: Splits one ulp between the final rounding and the constant's own truncation error, which fixes how many bits of pi you actually have to build.
source_headings: ## Multiplication of a fixed-point number by a real constant

notes.name: Fix-by-Real KCM
notes.description: KCM for an irrational constant: the shift is absorbed into each table's contents, all tables share one LSB, and g > log2(D) guard bits buy faithfulness.

notes.name: Periodic Shift-and-Add Rational Constant Multiplier
notes.description: Exploits the purely periodic binary expansion of A/B so each addition doubles the number of correct bits — i adders for 2^i repeats of the period.

notes.name: Rational-Constant KCM Table
notes.description: For a rational coefficient the KCM table is itself eventually periodic, so a 22-bit-wide table collapses to about alpha+s LUTs.

notes.name: Multiple Constant Multiplication
notes.description: One input, several coefficients, one fused adder graph — sharing intermediates that no per-constant optimum would ever reveal ({19,43} in three adders, not five).

notes.name: Pipelined Adder Graph
notes.description: Registers an MCM graph for throughput and minimises the balancing flops that then dominate cost — four registers instead of nine for {23,43}.

notes.name: Table-Based Multiple Constant Multiplication
notes.description: Shares identical LUT contents between constant multipliers — 52 distinct 1-bit tables cover every signed product by every constant up to 2^12.

notes.name: Sum of Constant Products
notes.description: Many inputs, one output — literally the transposed MCM graph, obtained by reversing every edge so branches become adders and adders become branches.

notes.name: Constant Matrix Multiplier
notes.description: Several inputs and several outputs optimised as one graph — a complex multiply by 19+43j in six adders where two MCM blocks need eight.

notes.name: KCM-Based Sum of Products
notes.description: Fuses every table of every tap into one bit heap with a single final rounding, so g > log2(ND) guard bits replace one rounding per multiplier.
source_headings: ### Table-based sum of products by real constants

notes.name: DSP-Block Constant Multiplier
notes.description: Splits the coefficient as c_Low +/- 2^B c_High across a cascaded DSP pair; the free choice of B lets a filter share sub-constants and drop ten DSPs to seven.

notes.name: Reconfigurable Constant Coefficient Multiplier
notes.description: Fuses the adder graphs of a small coefficient set into one graph with MUXes on the adder inputs — C in {45,19} for two adders and two MUXes.

notes.name: Recip Constant Divider
notes.description: Exact floor(X/D) as floor((AX+B)/2^p) — one constant multiplication and a shift; the only constant divider whose cost ignores the magnitude of D, at O(w^2) area and O(log w) delay.

notes.name: Constant Division Digit Table
notes.description: The (k+r)-in, (k+r)-out table that divides one radix-2^k digit prefixed by an incoming remainder; D*2^k useful entries, size independent of w, the loop body of every table-based constant divider.

notes.name: Sequential Constant Divider
notes.description: One table plus a remainder register clocked m = ceil(w/k) times; area constant in w, one operand in flight, remainder free because it is the state.

notes.name: LinArch Divider
notes.description: The recurrence unrolled into m chained tables — no adder anywhere on the datapath, area and delay both linear in w, and it pipelines to one exact quotient-and-remainder per cycle.

notes.name: Remainder-Only LinArch
notes.description: X mod D by dropping the quotient outputs from every table: area falls by the predictable factor r/(r+k), delay is unchanged because the remainder chain is the critical path.

notes.name: Binary Tree Constant Divider
notes.description: BTCD: the same exact division restructured from a chain into a tree — latency logarithmic in w instead of linear, at area proportional to w log w.
source_headings: > [!warning] Not covered in the source — needs outside research

notes.name: Remainder-Only BTCD
notes.description: X mod D as a clean binary tree of 2r-input, r-output tables; the quotient-assembly logic disappears so both area and delay improve — the right circuit whenever only the residue is wanted.

notes.name: Composite Constant Divider
notes.description: Divide by D = Da*Db as two chained dividers plus a multiply-add for R = Da*Rb + Ra; turns a table exponential in ra+rb into two tables exponential in ra and rb separately.

notes.name: Folded Array Squarer
notes.description: Halves a multiplier's AND-gate count and bit heap by folding the symmetric partial-product array onto one triangle plus a free diagonal of wires.

notes.name: High-Radix Squarer
notes.description: Splits X into k-bit subwords so the shared cross product X1*X0 is built once, cutting a 2-way split from 4 DSPs to 3 and a 3-way split from 9 to 6 with no extra additions.

notes.name: DSP-Cascade Squarer
notes.description: Rewrites the two-way split so all shift amounts become multiples of 17, letting the AMD DSP cascade carry the partial sum; costs one pre-shift of X1 and caps X at 33 bits.

notes.name: Booth-Recoded Squarer
notes.description: Applies radix-4 Booth digits to the folded square, shrinking the heap by about 3/4 but paying for a recoder and a Zi*Zj function; usually loses to the plain folded squarer.

notes.name: Truncated Squarer
notes.description: Drops the low heap columns and injects a compensation constant for a faithful result; because every squarer column is half a multiplier's, it truncates one column further for the same ulp budget.

notes.name: Squarer Tiling
notes.description: Covers only the on-and-above-diagonal region of the square with heterogeneous tiles, with each mirrored tile pair realised by one physical multiplier shifted left by 1; an ILP picks the cover (53-bit square in 4 DSPs).

notes.name: Squarer Staircase Tile
notes.description: A squarer-only staircase tile spanning diagonal and off-diagonal products, covering 15 partial products in 10 LUT5 (5 LUT6) at 1.43 PP/LUT — better than any LUT-based multiplier tile.

notes.name: Diagonal-Straddling Squarer Tile
notes.description: A rectangular DSP tile deliberately placed across the diagonal so it double-covers a square of bits, which is then recomputed and subtracted from the heap — worth it when the DSP covers a large area.

notes.name: Cube Bit Heap
notes.description: Direct binary expansion of X^3 into diagonal wires, xi*xj pairs and xi*xj*xk triples; the factor 3 does not fold, so the heap grows as the cube of the input width and only truncation makes it usable.
source_headings: ## Cubes and higher powers: direct algebraic expression

notes.name: Square-and-Multiply Power Chain
notes.description: Builds X^p from floor(log2 p) squarers and popcount(p)-1 multipliers; operator count is logarithmic in p but exact widths double at every stage.
source_headings: ## Cubes and higher powers: computing powers by squaring and multiplying

notes.name: Faithful Fixed-Point Power
notes.description: Runs the same recursion with |X|<1 and every intermediate clamped to the output width plus one guard bit per operation, using truncated squarers and multipliers so widths stay constant down the chain.
source_headings: ## Cubes and higher powers: approximate fixed-point powers

notes.name: Floating-Point Multiplier by a Power of Two
notes.description: Multiplying by 2^E_C collapses to one exponent add and exception logic — the significand path disappears entirely, at zero error.
source_headings: ### Multiplication by a power of two

notes.name: Faithful Floating-Point Constant Multiplier
notes.description: One known operand deletes the bias subtractor, the sign XOR and the two-operand multiplier; at most one bit of normalization is ever needed, for 1 ulp.
source_headings: ### The baseline faithful multiplier by a constant

notes.name: Product Normalization Predictor
notes.description: A constant comparator on the input fraction alone that decides normalization in parallel with the significand path, taking exponent update off the critical path.
source_headings: ### The baseline faithful multiplier by a constant

notes.name: Correctly Rounded Floating-Point Constant Multiplier
notes.description: Same architecture with an exact constant multiplier on 2+w_F+k bits, giving bit-for-bit IEEE results so an HLS compiler may legally substitute it.
source_headings: ### Correctly rounded multiplication by a floating-point constant

notes.name: Pseudo-Sticky Tie Anticipation
notes.description: Replaces the sticky path of round-to-nearest-even with a precomputed test on F_X, after a parity argument proves most tie cases impossible.
source_headings: ### Correctly rounded multiplication by a floating-point constant

notes.name: Floating-Point Multiplier by a Rational Constant
notes.description: An exclusion-zone theorem fixes the truncation width of A/B at w_F+1+ceil(log2 B), making correctly rounded multiplication by 1/3 or 3/10 cheap.
source_headings: ### Correct rounding of multiplication by a rational constant

notes.name: Saturated Normalizer
notes.description: An LZC-plus-shifter whose left shift saturates at the constant exponent E_C instead of w_F — one log factor shallower than a generic subnormal normalizer.

notes.name: Constant Multiplier with Subnormal Support
notes.description: Full subnormal handling for x*C: a pre-multiplier saturated normalizer when C>1, a post-multiplier right shift when C<1 which forfeits the merged-rounding trick.

notes.name: Floating-Point Divider by a Small Odd Constant
notes.description: Wraps a Euclidean constant divider in one small exponent adder and one significand mux; the normalization decision is an E_D-bit compare against F_D.
source_headings: ## Floating-point division by a small integer constant
### The baseline operator for normalized inputs

notes.name: Dividend Bias Rounding
notes.description: Round-to-nearest for free: pre-load H=(D-1)/2 into the low bits the normalization shift already zeroed, deleting the rounding adder's area and latency both.
source_headings: ### The baseline operator for normalized inputs

notes.name: Floating-Point Power Operator
notes.description: X^p as a p-bit normalization plus a square-and-multiply significand chain, with the exponent handled by a small constant multiplier off the critical path.

notes.name: Positive-Term Floating-Point Adder
notes.description: Guaranteed same-sign operands make the close path unreachable, so the LZC, the left normalizer and the path mux all vanish — about a third of the adder, at no accuracy cost.

notes.name: Fused Add-Subtract Unit
notes.description: X+Y and X-Y from one operand decode and one alignment shifter: a 3-path architecture (one close, two far) instead of two whole adders.

notes.name: Fused Multiply-Add
notes.description: One rounding of A*B+C instead of two: bounds the error against the result rather than the intermediate, paid for by a ~3w_F-bit internal datapath.
source_headings: ## Fused multiply-add and other sums of products

notes.name: Fused Sum of Squares
notes.description: Squares are positive by construction, so cancellation cannot occur and a faithfully rounded fusion saves both area and latency over separate multipliers and adders.
source_headings: ## Fused multiply-add and other sums of products

notes.name: Divide-by-Self Specialization
